p: The first words may be a title for the whole book, or for the opening section on John and the testing.
b: Mark has no birth story and no family tree. He starts with a phrase that has no verb: "The beginning of the good news." Readers take it three ways. (1) It is the title of the whole book: everything that follows is only the beginning of a good news that goes on in the church's preaching (13:10; 14:9). (2) It heads the first section, 1:1–13 or 1:1–15: John's work and Jesus' baptism and testing are the starting point of the good news. (3) It echoes "In the beginning" (Genesis 1:1, where the Greek Old Testament also has archē), so that God's new creation starts here, as John 1:1 would later say more openly. The readings can overlap. Many scholars also see a deliberate open end: a book that starts with "the beginning" and stops at 16:8 with fearful women may mean the story is not finished until the reader carries it on.

p: Euangelion meant a public announcement of victory or of an emperor's birth. Mark uses it for Jesus.
b: The Greek euangelion is the word behind the English "gospel" (Old English god spel, "good story"). This site translates it "good news." In the Greek Old Testament the verb is used of the herald who announces that God is coming back to reign: "Zion, you messenger of good news!" (Isaiah 40:9; compare Isaiah 52:7; 61:1). In the Roman world the word announced victories and the birthdays and accessions of emperors. A calendar inscription from Priene in Asia Minor (9 BC) says the birth of Augustus was "the beginning of the good news" for the world. Mark's readers in the empire would hear a challenge: the true good news is about Jesus. Mark is the first known writer to call a written account of Jesus "good news," and from the 100s the word became the name for this kind of book.

t: Christ: a title that became a name
p: Christos is Greek for the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one." Here it already works almost as a name.
b: Christos translates the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed," the word for kings and priests who were anointed with oil (1 Samuel 24:6; Leviticus 4:3) and, in Jesus' time, for the king many Jews hoped God would send. In 1:1, with no article, it is part of a name, "Jesus Christ," as in Paul's letters, so the Plain says "Christ." Where the Gospel uses it as a title, "the Messiah," the Plain says so (8:29; 14:61; 15:32). Mark's story slowly shows what kind of Messiah Jesus is: Peter names him at 8:29, Jesus forbids him to spread it, and he openly accepts the title only at his trial (14:61–62).

t: God's Son: the frame of the Gospel
p: Mark names Jesus God's Son at the start, God says it at the baptism and the transfiguration, and a centurion at the cross.
b: If the phrase belongs here (see the variant), Mark tells the reader at once what the characters in the story struggle to see. The title then returns at key points: the voice from heaven at the baptism (1:11), the shrieks of the unclean spirits (3:11; 5:7), the voice at the transfiguration (9:7), the high priest's question (14:61) and, finally, a Roman centurion who watches Jesus die (15:39). No human in the story calls him God's Son before the cross. In the Old Testament "son of God" can mean Israel (Exodus 4:22), the king (Psalm 2:7) or angels (Job 1:6); for Mark it means more than a title of office, though he never explains it in the later language of the creeds.

a: Look, I am sending my messenger before your face
p: Mark credits the quotation to Isaiah, but its first half comes from Exodus 23:20 and Malachi 3:1.
b: The first line joins two texts. In Exodus 23:20 God tells Israel in the wilderness, "Here, I am sending an angel in front of you" (the Hebrew mal'akh means both "angel" and "messenger"). In Malachi 3:1 God promises to send "my messenger" to clear the road before he comes to his Temple, a messenger Malachi 4:5 calls Elijah. Mark changes "before me" to "before your face," so the road is now prepared for someone else: Jesus. Then 1:3 quotes Isaiah 40:3. Jewish teachers often joined texts that share a key word ("road"), and Mark names only the greatest prophet, whose theme, God's return to his people through the wilderness, governs the whole. Matthew and Luke move the Malachi line to a later saying (Matthew 11:10; Luke 7:27). See the variant on "in Isaiah the prophet."
r: Exodus 23:20; Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5; Isaiah 40:3; Matthew 11:10; Luke 7:27

a: A voice is shouting in the wilderness
t: Isaiah 40:3, as the Greek reads it
p: In the Hebrew the road is built in the wilderness. In the Greek, which Mark follows, the voice is there.
b: Isaiah 40 opens the prophet's message of comfort to exiles in Babylon: God is coming home to Zion through the desert. This site's Plain of the Hebrew reads, "In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD!" (Isaiah 40:3): the road is built in the wilderness. The Greek Old Testament can be read so that the voice is in the wilderness, and Mark quotes it that way, which fits John's preaching in the desert (1:4). The community at Qumran used the same verse to explain why they had gone into the wilderness to study the Law (Community Rule 8:12–16). Mark also changes the last words: Isaiah's "for our God" becomes "for him," so that "the Lord" of the next line can be Jesus. Matthew 3:3, Luke 3:4 and John 1:23 quote the same verse.

p: In Isaiah the road is for the LORD, Israel's God. Mark applies it to Jesus without explaining.
b: The Greek kyrios, "Lord," stands in the Greek Old Testament for the divine name YHWH, which this site prints as "the LORD" in Old Testament books. In the New Testament the Greek has no divine name, so the Plain says "the Lord" (never "the LORD") even in quotations. Here the switch matters. Isaiah's road was for Israel's God coming home; John prepares the road for Jesus. Mark makes the claim quietly: the coming of Jesus is the coming of the Lord. Scholars such as Richard Bauckham and Joel Marcus see this as one of the earliest signs that the first Christians placed Jesus within the identity of Israel's one God.

p: The Jewish historian Josephus also tells of John, "surnamed the Baptist," and his death at Herod Antipas' order.
b: Mark first calls him ho baptizōn, "the one who baptizes," and later also uses the noun "the Baptist" (6:25; 8:28). Outside the Gospels, Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 18.116–119, written about AD 94) describes John as a good man who urged Jews to live justly and to come to baptism, and says that Herod Antipas feared his influence and had him killed at the fortress of Machaerus. Josephus adds that John's baptism was not meant to win pardon for sins but to purify the body once the soul had been cleansed by right living. Historians weigh this against Mark's "for sins to be forgiven"; many think Josephus is shaping John for Roman readers. See the topic page on John the Baptist.

p: Jews knew washings for purity. John's single, public immersion at his hands, for turning back to God, was new.
b: Jews of the time washed often for ritual purity, and many stepped pools (mikva'ot) have been found in Judea and Galilee. The Qumran community bathed daily and said that water cleanses only those who have turned from evil (Community Rule 3:4–9; 5:13–14). John's baptism differed: it was done once, in the open river, by John himself, and it marked repentance, a turning of the whole life back to God, in preparation for the one coming after him. Later Christians debated how John's baptism related to their own (Acts 18:25; 19:1–5); see the card on Matthew 3.

a: with a leather belt tied around his waist
p: John's clothing matches the description of Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8.
b: When King Ahaziah's messengers described the prophet who met them, they said he had "a leather loincloth tied around his waist" (2 Kings 1:8), and the king knew it was Elijah. Malachi had promised that God would send Elijah before the great day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). Mark never says outright that John is Elijah, but he lets the clothing speak, and later Jesus says that "Elijah has come" and was treated as people wished (9:11–13). A hairy cloak was also the mark of a prophet (Zechariah 13:4).

p: Locusts were clean food under the Law, and wild honey came from wild bees or perhaps date palms.
b: Leviticus 11:22 allows Israelites to eat locusts, and the Damascus Document from the Qumran sect gives rules for cooking them (Damascus Document 12:14–15). People in the Arabian and Judean deserts ate them dried or roasted. "Wild honey" was honey from wild bees in rocks and trees (Judges 14:8; 1 Samuel 14:25–27), or possibly the sap of date palms or trees. The point is not diet but distance: John lives on what the wilderness gives, outside the towns and the Temple economy.

a: The one stronger than I am
p: John's word "stronger" comes back in Jesus' picture of tying up the strong man (3:27).
b: John does not name the one who is coming. Readers of Isaiah would recall that the Lord God "comes with might" (Isaiah 40:10) and that he takes the captives of the strong (Isaiah 49:24–25). Mark plants the word: in 3:27 Jesus speaks of a "strong man" whose house cannot be robbed until someone ties him up. The one stronger than John proves stronger than Satan. Commentators such as Joel Marcus point out the link; Mark's readers would hear the story as a contest of strength.

a: untie the strap of his sandals
p: Untying a master's sandals was a slave's job. Later rabbis said a disciple need not do even that for his teacher.
b: Sandals were tied with leather thongs, and taking them off and washing the dusty feet was work for a household slave. A saying in the Babylonian Talmud (Ketubot 96a), credited to Rabbi Joshua ben Levi, says a disciple should do for his teacher every task a slave does, except untie his sandal. The saying is centuries later than Mark, but it shows how low the task ranked. John, a famous prophet with disciples of his own, says he is not worthy of even the slave's lowest work for the one coming after him. Mark adds "bend down," a vivid detail Matthew 3:11 lacks.

p: The prophets promised that God would pour out his Spirit. Mark's John has no "and fire," which Matthew and Luke add.
b: Israel's prophets pictured a coming day when God would pour out his Spirit like water on his people (Isaiah 44:3; Joel 2:28) and wash and renew their hearts (Ezekiel 36:25–27). John's water baptism points to that greater immersion. Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16 read "in the Holy Spirit and fire," with a warning of judgment; Mark has only the Spirit. Some scholars take Mark's shorter form as the older one; others, James Dunn among them, argue that John himself spoke of "Spirit and fire," a cleansing that is also judgment, and that Mark shortened it. Mark never tells of a later Spirit baptism, but Jesus promises the Spirit will speak through his followers on trial (13:11). Acts 1:5 and 11:16 tie John's saying to Pentecost; the questions about Spirit baptism are treated at Acts 2.
r: Isaiah 44:3; Joel 2:28; Ezekiel 36:25–27; Matthew 3:11; Luke 3:16; John 1:33; Acts 1:5; Acts 11:16; 13:11

p: Nazareth is never named in the Old Testament, Josephus or early rabbinic writings. It was a small farming village.
b: Nazareth lay in the hills of lower Galilee, about four miles from the rebuilt city of Sepphoris. It is not mentioned in the Old Testament, in Josephus or in the Mishnah, and the first mention outside Christian writings is a Hebrew inscription found at Caesarea in 1962, listing the priestly families that settled in Galilee after AD 135. Excavations show a village of a few hundred people with farms, cisterns and tombs. Mark says Jesus came "from Nazareth," and the name stuck: "Jesus of Nazareth" (1:24; 10:47; 14:67; 16:6). Mark mentions no birth in Bethlehem.

p: Mark tells the baptism without comment. Matthew adds John's protest, and Luke and John tell it more quietly.
b: Mark simply says that John baptized Jesus. That raised a question for the first Christians: if John's baptism was for repentance and forgiveness (1:4), why did the sinless Jesus receive it? Matthew adds John's protest and Jesus' answer about fulfilling all righteousness (Matthew 3:14–15); Luke mentions the baptism in a passing clause (Luke 3:21); John's Gospel does not narrate it at all. Historians call this a strong case of the "criterion of embarrassment": a story the church found awkward is unlikely to have been invented. The meanings Christians have found in it (Jesus standing with sinful Israel, obeying God, making water holy) are set out at Matthew 3; see the card there.

p: Mark's Greek says Jesus was baptized "into" the Jordan, a hint that he went down into the water.
b: Mark writes eis ton Iordanēn, literally "into the Jordan." In Mark's Greek eis can mean simply "in," and English versions differ. Many readers take it as a picture of immersion, which fits "stepping up out of the water" in 1:10. The verb baptizō itself means to dip or plunge, though in Mark 7:4 it is used of washing cups and pots. How baptism should be done (immersion, pouring or sprinkling) is debated among churches; Mark's words are evidence used by those who immerse.

p: Mark uses euthys, "immediately, right away," more than forty times. It gives his story its breathless pace.
b: Euthys appears in Mark more than forty times, more than in all the rest of the New Testament together. It often means "at once," but sometimes it works like "and then" or "so," moving the reader quickly to the next scene: eleven times in chapter 1 alone. The Plain usually renders it "right away" or "at once," and occasionally leaves it in a smoother phrase ("Just then," 1:23). Matthew and Luke drop most of these. Readers have called Mark the Gospel "in a hurry": a short book, mostly action, rushing toward the cross, which takes up a third of it.

p: Matthew and Luke say the heavens "opened." Mark uses a violent word, schizō, "split, tear."
b: Mark's word schizō means to split or tear, as cloth is torn (2:21 uses the noun for a "tear") or rocks are split (Matthew 27:51). Isaiah once prayed, "If only you would rip open the heavens and come down" (Isaiah 64:1), and Mark may mean that the prayer is answered: God has broken through. The same verb comes once more in Mark, at the moment Jesus dies, when the curtain of the Temple is torn in two from top to bottom (15:38). Readers have long seen these two splittings as a frame around the whole story, at the baptism a voice says "You are my Son," and at the cross a centurion says that Jesus was God's Son. Codex Bezae (D) and many Latin copies change the word to "opened," as in Matthew and Luke.

p: The dove has been linked to the Spirit over the waters at creation, to Noah's dove, and to Israel.
b: Mark does not explain the image, and readers have offered several. (1) Creation: God's Spirit "fluttered over the face of the waters" (Genesis 1:2), and a saying in the Babylonian Talmud (Hagigah 15a) compares that hovering to a dove; the baptism would be a new creation. (2) Noah: after the flood a dove brought an olive leaf, a sign of a new world (Genesis 8:8–12). (3) Israel: later Jewish writings sometimes picture Israel as a dove (compare Psalm 74:19; Hosea 11:11). "Like a dove" may describe the way the Spirit came down, gently and from above, rather than its shape; Luke 3:22 says "in bodily shape, like a dove."
r: Genesis 1:2; Genesis 8:8–12; Psalm 74:19; Hosea 11:11; Matthew 3:16; Luke 3:22; John 1:32

p: Mark says the Spirit came down eis auton, "into him"; Matthew and Luke say "on him."
b: The best manuscripts of Mark read eis auton, "into him" or "to him," while the later Byzantine text and Matthew 3:16 have ep' auton, "upon him." In Mark's Greek eis sometimes means "on" or "toward," so the difference may be small. But several scholars (Robert Gundry, Joel Marcus) take Mark's wording seriously: the Spirit enters Jesus and from now on drives his work, beginning at once in 1:12. The Plain keeps "into him" so readers can see the choice.

a: You are my dearly loved Son
p: The voice combines the king of Psalm 2, Abraham's beloved son, and the servant in whom God delights.
b: Three Old Testament passages sound together. (1) Psalm 2:7, where God says to his anointed king, "You are my son." (2) Genesis 22:2, where God tells Abraham to take Isaac, "your only one, whom you love"; the Greek Old Testament calls Isaac Abraham's agapētos, "beloved" son, the same word Mark uses, so some hear a hint of sacrifice. (3) Isaiah 42:1, the servant of the LORD: "I have placed my Spirit on him." In Mark the voice speaks to Jesus ("You are"), and only Jesus is said to see the vision; in Matthew 3:17 it speaks about him ("This is"). The voice returns at the transfiguration, then addressed to the disciples (9:7).
r: Psalm 2:7; Genesis 22:2; Isaiah 42:1; 9:7; 12:6; Matthew 3:17; Luke 3:22; 2 Peter 1:17

p: Some early Christians read Mark to mean Jesus became God's Son at the Jordan. The church rejected that reading.
b: Because Mark begins with the baptism, some early groups read it as the moment Jesus was adopted as God's Son. Irenaeus (about 180) says that those who "separate Jesus from Christ," teaching that the Christ came down on the man Jesus at the baptism and left him before the cross, preferred Mark's Gospel (Against Heresies 3.11.7). The view later called adoptionism was condemned. Most readers, ancient and modern, note that the voice does not say "Today you have become my Son" (as some copies of Luke 3:22 do, quoting Psalm 2:7 in full) but declares what already is: "You are." The Greek past tense eudokēsa ("I took delight") is commonly read as timeless. Mark 1:1 has already named Jesus God's Son before the baptism.

p: Mark uses ekballō, the same verb as for throwing out demons. Matthew and Luke soften it to "led."
b: Ekballō is the word Mark uses again and again for Jesus throwing demons out (1:34, 39; 3:15, 22–23). Here the Spirit who has just come into Jesus throws him out into the wilderness. The verb is strong; it is not a gentle leading but a forceful sending, almost a compulsion. Matthew 4:1 and Luke 4:1 change it to "led," one of many places where the later Gospels smooth Mark's rough edges. Mark also tells this in the present tense ("the Spirit throws him out"), a lively storytelling habit the Plain usually turns into the past.

p: Moses spent forty days on the mountain, Elijah traveled forty days to Horeb, and Israel spent forty years in the wilderness.
b: The number calls up Israel's story. Moses was on the mountain with the LORD "forty days and forty nights" (Exodus 34:28). Elijah, fed by an angel, walked forty days to the mountain of God (1 Kings 19:8). Israel wandered forty years, so that God could test them "to know what was in your heart" (Deuteronomy 8:2). Mark tells the testing in only two verses and does not describe the three tests that Matthew and Luke report (Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13), nor does he say Jesus fasted. He gives no result: the contest with Satan goes on through the whole Gospel, in the exorcisms and even in Peter's words (8:33).

p: Mark uses "Satan" (a Hebrew word, "adversary") for the leader of evil, never "the devil."
b: Satan comes from the Hebrew satan, "adversary, accuser." In Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3 ha-satan, "the Accuser," is a member of God's court; by the time of Jesus "Satan" had become the name of the chief enemy of God and his people. Mark always calls him Satan (1:13; 3:23, 26; 4:15; 8:33), while Matthew and Luke also say "the devil." In Mark, Satan's rule shows itself in unclean spirits, illness and blindness to God's ways, and Jesus' work is the binding of the "strong man" (3:27).

a: He was out among the wild animals
p: Danger, a new Adam at peace with creation, or a word to Christians thrown to beasts in Rome? Mark alone has it.
b: Only Mark mentions the wild animals, and readers take the detail in three ways. (1) Danger: the desert was the haunt of jackals, hyenas and snakes, and Psalm 91 promises the faithful one that he will tread on lion and cobra (Psalm 91:11–13), with angels to guard him. (2) Peace: Jesus is a new Adam living at peace with the animals, as in the promised age when "the wolf will stay as a guest with the lamb" (Isaiah 11:6); the Testament of Naphtali (8:4) promises that for the righteous the devil will flee, the wild beasts will fear them and the angels will stand by them. Richard Bauckham argues for this reading. (3) Rome: Christians under Nero were dressed in animal skins and torn apart by dogs (Tacitus, Annals 15.44); Mark's readers may have found comfort in a Lord who had faced beasts and was served by angels.

a: the angels kept taking care of him
p: As an angel fed Elijah in the wilderness, angels care for Jesus. The verb is the same as the "serving" in 1:31.
b: In the desert an angel woke Elijah and fed him for his forty-day journey (1 Kings 19:5–8), and Psalm 91:11 promises angels to guard the faithful. The Greek diēkonoun, "they were serving," is the verb used of Simon's mother-in-law (1:31) and of the women at the cross (15:41), and Jesus will say that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (10:45). The imperfect tense suggests ongoing care during the forty days, not only at the end as in Matthew 4:11.

a: After John had been handed over
p: The verb paradidōmi is used of John, then of Jesus, then of his followers: one path from preaching to suffering.
b: Mark does not yet say who handed John over or why; the story comes in 6:17–29. The verb paradidōmi, "hand over," returns at key points: Judas will hand Jesus over (3:19; 14:10), the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and the Gentiles (9:31; 10:33), and Jesus' followers will be handed over to councils and kings (13:9–12). The pattern of John, then Jesus, then the disciples tells Mark's readers that preaching the good news leads through suffering. Matthew 4:12 keeps the same verb.

p: Kairos means the decisive moment, not clock time. God's appointed hour has come.
b: Greek has two common words for time: chronos, time as it passes, and kairos, the right or decisive moment. Jesus uses kairos: the season God appointed has reached its fullness. Readers of Daniel would think of the times set before God's kingdom comes (Daniel 7:22; Daniel 9:24–27), and Paul writes that God sent his Son when the fullness of time had come (Galatians 4:4). The perfect tense says the time stands fulfilled. Only Mark has this first line; Matthew 4:17 gives just the call to repent.

a: the kingdom of God has drawn near
p: Has God's kingdom arrived, or is it about to? Scholars have argued over this verb for a century.
b: The kingdom (or reign) of God means God ruling as king, as Israel's psalms and prophets longed for (Psalm 145:11–13; Isaiah 52:7; Daniel 2:44). Matthew prefers "kingdom of heaven," a Jewish way of saying the same thing. The verb ēngiken means "has come near." C. H. Dodd argued it means "has arrived" (realized eschatology); Albert Schweitzer and others read it as "is about to come" (future eschatology); many today hold both: in Jesus' work the kingdom is already breaking in (3:27), yet its full coming is still ahead (9:1; 14:25). See the topic page on the kingdom of God.
orig: ἤγγικεν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ (ēngiken hē basileia tou theou)

p: A freshwater lake about 13 miles long. Mark calls it a sea, as Hebrew did; Luke calls it a lake.
b: The Sea of Galilee (Hebrew Kinneret) is a freshwater lake about 13 miles long and 8 wide, some 700 feet below sea level. Mark and Matthew call it a "sea" (thalassa), following Hebrew usage, which calls any large body of water yam; Luke, writing for a wider Greek audience, calls it a "lake" (Luke 5:1). Fishing was a major business there: towns like Magdala salted and shipped fish, and the trade was taxed for Herod Antipas. In 1986 a fishing boat of about the first century was found in the mud near Ginosar, about 27 feet long, the kind of boat the disciples would have used.

p: In Jeremiah, God sends fishers to haul in a guilty people. Jesus turns the image toward gathering people for the kingdom.
b: The image had a history. In Jeremiah 16:16 God says he will send many fishers and hunters to catch the people of Judah for judgment, and Amos 4:2 and Habakkuk 1:14–17 use hooks and nets as pictures of capture. Jesus takes the trade of the men in front of him and gives it a new purpose: as they once gathered fish, they will now gather people for God's coming rule. Whether a note of judgment remains is debated; in Mark the call is mainly to mission (3:14; 6:7–13). The Greek adds "become" (Matthew 4:19 lacks it): they will grow into it.
r: Jeremiah 16:16; Amos 4:2; Habakkuk 1:14–17; Ezekiel 47:10; Matthew 4:19; Luke 5:10

a: Right away they dropped their nets and followed him
p: When Elijah called Elisha, Elisha asked to kiss his parents goodbye first. These men leave at once.
b: The scene echoes the call of Elisha. Elijah threw his cloak over Elisha as he plowed, and Elisha asked, "Please, let me kiss my father and my mother" (1 Kings 19:20) before following. Simon and Andrew, then James and John, leave at once, and James and John leave their father in the boat (1:20). In the Jewish world disciples usually chose a teacher and asked to study with him; here the teacher chooses and calls. Mark gives no reason for their response, so the weight falls on the authority of Jesus' word. John 1:35–42 suggests some had met Jesus earlier through John the Baptist.

t: Not the poorest of the poor
p: Zebedee had hired workers. Galilean fishing families could run small businesses with partners and laborers.
b: Only Mark mentions the hired workers. Fishing in Galilee was organized in family firms that leased fishing rights, owned boats and nets, and hired day laborers; Luke 5:10 says James and John were partners with Simon. So the first disciples were not destitute; they left a working business and their father. That cost is what Peter recalls later, when he says they have left everything to follow Jesus (10:28). It also means Zebedee was not left alone, a detail some readers think Mark included so the sons would not seem to abandon him.

p: A fishing town on the north shore of the lake, on the border of Antipas' territory. Its synagogue and houses have been dug up.
b: Capernaum (Hebrew Kefar Nahum, "Nahum's village") lay on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, near the border between the lands of Herod Antipas and his brother Philip, which explains a toll office there (2:14). It had perhaps a thousand people. Excavations show a white limestone synagogue from the late 300s or 400s AD, built over the black basalt foundations of an earlier building that many think was the synagogue of Jesus' time. Nearby lies a house that was turned into a place of Christian worship and later covered by an eight-sided church; many archaeologists think it was honored early as Peter's house (1:29). Jesus makes the town his base (2:1).

a: he was in the synagogue teaching
p: Synagogues were village meeting houses where the Law was read and explained on the Sabbath. Visitors could be asked to teach.
b: A synagogue (Greek for "gathering") was both the community and its building. On the Sabbath Jews met to read and explain the Law and the Prophets (Luke 4:16–21; Acts 13:14–15). An inscription found in Jerusalem, set up by a priest named Theodotus before AD 70, says his synagogue was built "for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments." Buildings from before 70 have been excavated at Gamla, Magdala and Masada. There was no fixed preacher; respected men, including visitors, could be invited to teach. Mark does not say what Jesus taught, only how: with authority (1:22).

p: Scribes taught by passing on and explaining tradition. Jesus spoke on his own authority. The contrast is not a caricature.
b: Scribes were the trained experts in the law of Moses: they copied, taught and applied it, and many were Pharisees (2:16). Their way of teaching was to pass on and explain what earlier teachers had said, as the Mishnah later does ("Rabbi so-and-so says..."). Jesus does not cite authorities; he speaks as one who has authority himself, and in this chapter his word even commands unclean spirits (1:27). Mark is not saying the scribes taught badly: Mark himself has a scribe whom Jesus praises (12:28–34). Jewish scholars such as Geza Vermes compare Jesus to charismatic holy men like Hanina ben Dosa, whose authority came from closeness to God rather than learning.

p: Mark often calls demons "unclean spirits," using the language of purity: the opposite of the Holy Spirit and the Holy One.
b: Mark uses "unclean spirit" eleven times and "demon" about as often, for the same beings. "Unclean" is Temple language: what is unclean cannot come near God's holiness. Mark sets up a contrast in 1:23–24: a man in an unclean spirit meets the one who has the Holy Spirit (1:8, 10) and whom the spirit calls "the Holy One of God." The phrase "in an unclean spirit" pictures the man as gripped, as if surrounded, by the spirit. Zechariah 13:2 had promised that God would remove "the unclean spirit" from the land. See the topic on fallen angels and demons.

a: What is there between us and you
t: "What is there between us and you?"
p: A Hebrew idiom meaning "Leave us alone" or "Why are you against us?" It was a way to fend someone off.
b: The phrase is a Semitic idiom, literally "What to us and to you?" It is used when one person resists another's interference: Jephthah to the Ammonite king (Judges 11:12) and the widow of Zarephath to Elijah (1 Kings 17:18). The spirit speaks in the plural "us," as if for all its kind: if Jesus is the stronger one, the whole realm of evil is in danger. The Byzantine text (followed by the KJV) begins with Ea, "Ha!" or "Let us alone," which is missing in Vaticanus and Bezae; the same word stands in the parallel in Luke 4:34.
orig: τί ἡμῖν καὶ σοί (ti hēmin kai soi)

a: I know who you are: the Holy One of God
t: Why does the spirit say his name?
p: In the ancient world, knowing a name gave power. The spirit may be trying to control Jesus, not praise him.
b: "The Holy One of God" recalls Aaron, "the LORD's holy one" (Psalm 106:16), and Elisha, "a holy man of God" (2 Kings 4:9); here it marks Jesus as God's own. Why would a demon say it? Ancient magical texts show exorcists trying to master a spirit by naming it, and spirits answering by naming the exorcist. Many scholars read the spirit's words as a defensive spell: "I know who you are." Jesus replies with a command to be silent (1:25), and wins. For Mark's readers the irony is plain: the spirits know who Jesus is, while people do not, and the spirits' knowledge does them no good. See the note on 1:34.

p: Jesus uses a rough word, "be muzzled," the same one he later uses to calm the storm (4:39).
b: Phimoō means to put a muzzle on an animal (1 Corinthians 9:9 uses it of oxen), and then to silence someone. Jesus does not argue with the spirit or use spells or tools, as other exorcists did; he gives two short commands. The same verb appears when Jesus speaks to the wind and the sea: "Be quiet! Be muzzled!" (4:39). Mark presents the storm as one more evil power that must obey, and the crowd's amazement that the spirits obey him (1:27) comes back there, when the disciples marvel that even the wind and the sea obey him (4:41).

p: Peter was married and lived in Capernaum. Excavators found a house there honored by Christians from early times.
b: Simon Peter had a wife (1 Corinthians 9:5 says she traveled with him) and a home in Capernaum, shared with his brother and his mother-in-law. John 1:44 says they came from Bethsaida. Beneath an eight-sided church of the 400s near the lake, Franciscan archaeologists found a room of a first-century house that was plastered and used for gatherings, with Christian graffiti from later centuries. Many scholars think it was venerated as Peter's house, though no inscription proves it. If so, Mark's readers met the first house church in this story.

p: Mark's verb for helping her up, egeirō, is the word for raising the dead, used again at Jesus' own resurrection.
b: Egeirō means "wake up, raise," and the New Testament uses it for resurrection. Mark uses it for Jesus lifting Peter's mother-in-law (1:31), for the paralyzed man ("Get up," 2:9, 11), for Jairus' daughter (5:41) and the boy who seemed dead (9:27), and finally for Jesus himself: "He has been raised" (16:6). Mark's readers, who had been "raised" with Christ in baptism, would hear in each healing a small picture of the resurrection.

p: Was she just making dinner? Mark uses the verb of discipleship: serving is what the Son of Man came to do (10:45).
b: Some readers see only a sign that the fever was gone: she could get up and cook. Others note that Mark uses diakoneō, "serve," with care: angels serve Jesus (1:13), the women at the cross had "served him" in Galilee (15:41), and Jesus says that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (10:45). On that reading she is the first person in Mark to do what a disciple should, while the men will argue about who is greatest (9:34). Feminist and other scholars also note that her service happens in a house, the setting of Mark's early house churches. Both readings can stand: the healing is real, and her response is a model.

p: The Sabbath ended at sundown. Only then did people carry the sick to Jesus, since carrying was work.
b: Jewish days begin at sunset, so the Sabbath of 1:21 ended when the sun went down. The Law forbade work on the Sabbath, and Jeremiah 17:21–22 names carrying loads; the Mishnah's list of the thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work ends with carrying from one place to another (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2). So the townspeople waited until evening to carry their sick. Mark doubles the time phrase ("as evening came on, when the sun went down") to make the point. The scene foreshadows the Sabbath debates of 2:23–3:6.

a: He would not let the demons speak
p: Jesus silences demons, healed people and disciples about who he is. William Wrede called this the messianic secret.
b: Again and again in Mark, Jesus commands silence: to demons (1:25, 34; 3:12), to people he heals (1:44; 5:43; 7:36; 8:26) and to his disciples (8:30; 9:9). In 1901 William Wrede argued that this was Mark's (or his tradition's) device to explain why Jesus had not been recognized as Messiah in his lifetime. Others reply that Jesus really did avoid popular titles that would have been misunderstood as a call to revolt; that the secret serves Mark's point that Jesus can be understood only through the cross (9:9); and that many commands are broken at once (1:45; 7:36), so the secret is more about the nature of his messiahship than about hiding it. See the book's introduction.

p: Mark shows Jesus praying three times, each at night and at a turning point: here, after the feeding (6:46), and in Gethsemane.
b: Mark rarely shows Jesus praying, and each time it is in darkness and alone, at a moment of decision: after his first great success (1:35), after feeding the five thousand (6:46) and in Gethsemane (14:32–39). Each time the disciples are close by and do not understand. Here they come "hunting" for him (1:36), wanting him back where the crowds are; Jesus instead moves on. The "deserted place" (erēmos topos) uses the word for wilderness (1:3–4, 12–13): Jesus returns to where he met his Father and was tested.

a: This is what I came out for
p: Jesus may mean he left Capernaum for this purpose, or that he came out from God. Luke reads it the second way.
b: The verb exēlthon, "I came out," may simply refer to his leaving the house before dawn (1:35): "this is why I went out," to preach elsewhere, not to stay as a local healer. But in Luke's version Jesus says that this is why he was sent (Luke 4:43), and John often has Jesus say he "came out from God" (John 8:42; 16:28). Many commentators think Mark's wording leaves room for the larger meaning: Jesus' mission is to preach the kingdom everywhere. The Byzantine text has the perfect "I have come forth," pointing the same way.

a: A man with a skin disease
p: The Greek lepros means someone with the skin disease of Leviticus 13, not Hansen's disease. The issue was impurity.
b: Lepros is the Greek Old Testament's word for a person with tsara'at, the skin disease of Leviticus 13–14, which this site renders "skin disease." It covered many flaking or spreading conditions, and even mold in cloth and houses. Modern leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a different illness. The problem in the Law was impurity: the person lived outside the camp, wore torn clothes and called out "Unclean! Unclean!" (Leviticus 13:45–46). So the man asks to be made clean, not just cured. Healing such a person was thought as hard as raising the dead (2 Kings 5:7). Parallels: Matthew 8:1–4; Luke 5:12–16.
r: Leviticus 13:45–46; Leviticus 14:1–32; Numbers 12:10–15; 2 Kings 5:1–14; 2 Kings 5:7; Matthew 8:1–4; Luke 5:12–16

p: Touching a person with skin disease made you unclean. Here the cleanness passes the other way.
b: Under the Law, touching an unclean person made one unclean until evening (Leviticus 5:3; compare Numbers 5:2). Uncleanness was not sin; it was a state that kept a person from the Temple and was removed by washing, waiting and offerings. Jesus could have healed by a word. He touches first, and instead of the impurity passing to him, the cleanness passes to the man. Jewish scholars such as Paula Fredriksen point out that Jesus does not reject the purity system here: he sends the man straight to the priest (1:44), and no one in the story objects to the touch. See the note on Matthew 8:3.

a: Jesus spoke to him harshly and drove him away
p: Two strong verbs: Jesus "snorted" at the man and "threw him out." Matthew and Luke leave both out.
b: Embrimaomai was used of horses snorting, and of people who scold or are deeply stirred (14:5; John 11:33, 38). Ekballō is the verb for throwing out demons (1:34, 39). Together they make a startling scene, and both Matthew 8:4 and Luke 5:14 omit them. Explanations vary: Jesus is still moved by the anger of 1:41 (see the variant there); he is sternly impressing the order to keep silent; or he is sending the man away at once, out of the house or the town, to the priest. The strong words fit Mark's habit of showing Jesus' emotions, which the other Gospels often soften.

p: Leviticus 14 lays out the rite for a person healed of skin disease: a priest's inspection, two birds, washing and offerings.
b: Leviticus 14 begins, "This is the procedure for a person with skin disease on the day he is made clean" (Leviticus 14:2). A priest examined the person outside the camp, then performed a rite with two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn and hyssop. After washing, shaving and seven days' wait, the person brought lambs (or birds, if poor) as offerings at the sanctuary. In Jesus' day the offerings would be made at the Temple in Jerusalem. Jesus keeps the Law here: the man's healing must be confirmed by the priest so that he can go back to his family and community.

t: Evidence for them, or against them?
p: The phrase can mean proof to the priests that he is clean, or testimony against them. Mark uses it elsewhere of witness against.
b: Eis martyrion autois can mean "as evidence for them," that is, proof to the priests and the people that the man is clean and may rejoin society; or "as a testimony to them" about Jesus, the one who cleanses; or even "as evidence against them," as when the disciples shake dust off their feet "as evidence against them" (6:11) or testify before rulers (13:9). Most scholars take the first sense as the main one in this verse, with the second in the background. Matthew 8:4 and Luke 5:14 keep the phrase without explaining it.

a: Jesus was no longer able to go openly into a town
t: The cleansed man and the outcast Jesus
p: The man who lived outside towns now goes in and preaches. Jesus, who touched him, must stay outside.
b: Mark tells the ending with irony. The man with the skin disease had to live outside the towns (Leviticus 13:46). Now he goes in, "preaching" (Mark's word for what John, Jesus and the Twelve do, 1:4, 14; 3:14) and spreading "the message." Jesus, who touched him, ends up outside, in deserted places, as if he had taken the man's place. Some readers see a first picture of the exchange at the heart of the passion, where the clean one is put outside. Others stress that the man disobeys a clear command (1:44), and that Mark is showing how hard it is to keep Jesus' work hidden.

p: Ho logos, literally "the word," was an early Christian name for the message about Jesus. Mark uses it that way.
b: Jesus "spoke the message to them." The Greek is ho logos, literally "the word," used alone, without "God's" or "his": the way the early church spoke of its preaching (Acts 4:31; 8:4; 1 Thessalonians 1:6). The Plain renders it "the message" in Mark, so that readers can follow it: in the parable of the sower the message is what is sown (4:14–20), and Jesus spoke the message in parables (4:33). The healed man in 1:45 was already spreading "the message." Mark's readers would recognize their own preaching in Jesus' teaching.

p: Galilean roofs were beams covered with branches and packed mud. Luke, writing for city readers, says "tiles."
b: Houses in Galilean villages were built of rough basalt stones, with flat roofs of wooden beams covered with reeds or branches and a layer of packed clay, reached by an outside stair. Mark's words are earthy: they "unroofed the roof" and "dug through." Luke says they lowered the man "through the tiles" (Luke 5:19), the kind of roof his Greek readers knew. Many scholars see this as a small example of a later Gospel adapting Mark for a different audience. Mark's word for the mat, krabattos, is a common word for a poor person's pallet.

p: Jesus sees the faith of the four friends, perhaps with the man's. Faith in Mark is shown by action.
b: Mark says nothing about what the paralyzed man believed; Jesus sees "their" faith, the persistence of the friends who would not be stopped by a crowd or a roof. In Mark faith is not a set of ideas but trust that acts: the bleeding woman pushes through to touch Jesus' clothes (5:27–34), Bartimaeus keeps shouting (10:46–52). The verse has also been used in debates about whether the faith of others can benefit someone, for example in infant baptism, where the church or the parents bring the child. Readers on both sides of that debate agree that the verse shows the power of friends who bring someone to Jesus.

p: Many Jews linked illness with sin. Jesus does not say this man's illness came from sin, but he deals with both.
b: Jesus' first words surprise: the man came for healing and receives forgiveness. Some Jews of the time linked sickness and sin (Psalm 103:3; John 9:2), though the book of Job argues against a simple link. Jesus does not say the paralysis came from sin; he treats forgiveness as the deeper need. The passive "are forgiven" may be a "divine passive," meaning "God forgives you," which is how some interpreters explain the scribes' reaction: Jesus is declaring God's forgiveness as a prophet might (2 Samuel 12:13). But the scribes hear it as Jesus forgiving on his own authority, and Jesus' answer (2:10) claims exactly that authority for the Son of Man.
orig: ἀφίενταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι (aphientai sou hai hamartiai)

p: Jewish law defined blasphemy narrowly. The scribes' charge reflects a belief that only God forgives sins.
b: In the Torah blasphemy meant speaking "the name of the LORD with contempt" (Leviticus 24:16), and the Mishnah later says the blasphemer is guilty only if he pronounces the divine name itself (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:5). Jesus does neither. The scribes use the word loosely: he is claiming what belongs to God. Yet Jews of the time could speak of humans declaring forgiveness: priests did through sacrifice (Leviticus 4:20), and in the Prayer of Nabonidus from Qumran (4Q242) on one reading of the fragment a Jewish diviner "forgave" the king's sin, as Geza Vermes points out (others read it so that God forgives and the diviner only explains). The charge foreshadows the end: at his trial Jesus is condemned for blasphemy (14:64).

p: The scribes' words echo the Shema: "The LORD is one." Mark's Jesus will quote it in full (12:29).
b: The Greek heis ho theos, "one, God," recalls the daily prayer of Israel, the Shema: "Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). The scribes defend God's uniqueness, as faithful Jews should. Mark does not mock their concern; his Jesus later quotes the Shema in full and praises a scribe who affirms it (12:29–34). The tension Mark leaves for his readers is how Jesus can do what belongs to the one God without there being two Gods. The same phrase returns in 10:18.

p: Jesus' favorite way of speaking of himself. It can mean "a human being," and it recalls the heavenly figure of Daniel 7.
b: "Son of Man" (Aramaic bar enash) can mean simply "a human being," as often in Ezekiel and Psalm 8:4. In Daniel 7:13–14 "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds and receives authority and a kingdom from God. In Mark only Jesus uses the phrase, always of himself: here with authority on earth, then of his suffering (8:31; 9:31; 10:33, 45), then of his coming in glory (8:38; 13:26; 14:62). Geza Vermes argued that the Aramaic was a modest way of saying "I"; Daniel Boyarin argues that Jews already read Daniel 7 as a divine figure, so the title was a high claim. Notice "on earth": the Son of Man of Daniel's heavenly vision exercises God's authority here, among people.
orig: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (ho huios tou anthrōpou)

p: The crowd is ex-stasis, "standing outside themselves." In 3:21 Jesus' family says the same of him.
b: The verb existēmi means literally "to stand outside" oneself: to be amazed, or to be out of one's mind. Here the crowd is beside itself with wonder. In 3:21 the people close to Jesus say that he is "beside himself." The Plain uses the same English both times so that readers can see Mark's play: the power that amazes the crowds looks to some like madness. Paul uses the same word of himself: "If we are out of our minds, it is for God" (2 Corinthians 5:13).

p: Mark and Luke call the tax collector Levi. Matthew 9:9 tells the same story about "Matthew."
b: Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 tell of Levi son of Alphaeus; Matthew 9:9 tells the same scene with the name Matthew, and the lists of the Twelve (3:18; Matthew 10:3) include a Matthew but no Levi. Explanations: Levi and Matthew were one man with two names, like Simon Peter (the church's usual view); the author of Matthew swapped in the name of an apostle so the tax collector would be one of the Twelve (a common critical view); or two different people. James "son of Alphaeus" also appears in the list (3:18); whether he was Levi's brother is unknown. See the topic on Matthew.

t: A toll booth on the border
p: Capernaum sat on a trade road at the border of Antipas' land. Levi likely collected tolls on goods for him.
b: Levi was probably not a Roman tax official. In Galilee, Herod Antipas ruled under Rome, and tolls on goods crossing his border were farmed out to local collectors who paid in advance and then collected what they could. Capernaum lay on a road near the border with his brother Philip's territory, a natural place for a toll booth. Tax collectors were widely despised, both for dishonesty (Luke 3:12–13) and for working the system of a foreign-backed ruler. The Mishnah later allows a person to make a false vow to escape murderers, robbers and tax collectors (Mishnah Nedarim 3:4). Jesus calls one to follow him with the same words he used to the fishermen.

p: At banquets people lay on couches around the table. Sharing a meal meant accepting one another.
b: At formal meals in the Greek and Roman world, and among Jews who adopted the custom, guests lay on their left side on couches around a low table. Who ate with whom mattered greatly: a shared table meant friendship and acceptance. The Pharisees were known for careful rules about food and table companions, and they formed fellowships that ate in purity. Jesus' meals with tax collectors and sinners therefore made a public statement, as his opponents saw: "He overeats and he is a heavy wine drinker, a friend to tax collectors and sinners!" (Matthew 11:19). Mark's own churches met for meals in houses, where Jews and Gentiles ate together.

p: "His house" may be Levi's (as Luke says) or Jesus' own house in Capernaum (2:1).
b: The Greek says only "in his house." Luke 5:29 makes it clear that Levi gave a great banquet in his own house, and most readers follow that. But some scholars point out that in Mark the most recent "he" is Jesus, and that Jesus has just been "at home" in Capernaum (2:1). If the house is Jesus', then he is the host who invites tax collectors and sinners to his table, which sharpens the point. Mark's grammar allows both.
orig: ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ αὐτοῦ (en tē oikia autou)

p: Not ordinary people who were careless about purity, but those who broke God's law openly. Jesus ate with them.
b: Older Christian writing often said that the Pharisees despised ordinary Jews who did not keep their purity rules, and called them "sinners." E. P. Sanders challenged this: in Jewish sources "sinners" (Hebrew resha'im) means the wicked, people who flouted God's law, such as cheats and extortioners, not the common people (the am ha-aretz). If so, the offense of Jesus' meals was not that he ignored purity rules but that he welcomed the openly wicked without first requiring the usual signs of repentance (restitution, sacrifice). Others, such as Amy-Jill Levine, add that the Gospels' picture of Pharisees shunning all sinners should not be read as the stance of Judaism as a whole.

p: A lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the Law and the traditions of the elders. Their heirs shaped rabbinic Judaism.
b: The Pharisees (perhaps from Hebrew perushim, "separated ones") were a popular Jewish movement known for exact interpretation of the law of Moses and for keeping "the tradition of the elders" (7:3), including purity at meals and tithing. Josephus says they had great influence among the people and believed in the resurrection and in fate working with free will. Their heirs, the rabbis, compiled the Mishnah about AD 200. Mark's phrase "the scribes of the Pharisees" means scribes who belonged to the Pharisaic party. In Mark they are Jesus' main debate partners in Galilee, but they play almost no part in his death. The usual Christian picture of Pharisees as hypocrites does them injustice; see the topic page.
orig: οἱ γραμματεῖς τῶν Φαρισαίων (hoi grammateis tōn Pharisaiōn)

a: People who are strong do not need a doctor
t: The doctor goes to the sick
p: A saying with parallels in Greek philosophy: physicians spend their time among the sick.
b: Jesus answers with a proverb. Greek writers had similar sayings: Cynic philosophers were said to defend their mixing with bad company by answering that doctors spend their time among the sick without catching their fevers (Diogenes Laertius gives such a saying for Antisthenes). The second line explains it: "I did not come to call righteous people." Is that irony, since no one is truly righteous (Romans 3:10), or does it accept for the moment the Pharisees' own view of themselves? Readers differ. Matthew 9:13 adds a quotation of Hosea 6:6; Luke 5:32 adds "to repentance" (see the variant).
r: Matthew 9:12–13; Luke 5:31–32; Hosea 6:6; Luke 15:1–7; Luke 19:10; 1 Timothy 1:15

a: John's disciples and the Pharisees were keeping a fast
p: Pious Jews fasted on set days beyond the Day of Atonement. Later Christians fasted on Wednesdays and Fridays.
b: The Law required only one fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). Pious Jews added others: after disasters, in mourning, and in some groups twice a week (Luke 18:12). The Didache, an early Christian manual, tells believers not to fast with "the hypocrites" on Mondays and Thursdays but on Wednesdays and Fridays (Didache 8:1), which shows both the Jewish custom and how early Christians kept fasting while making it their own. John's disciples kept a stricter life (1:6). The question is why Jesus' disciples do not fast at all. See the card on fast days at Matthew 6.

p: The prophets pictured God as Israel's groom. Jesus casts himself as the groom whose presence turns fasting into a feast.
b: Literally "the sons of the bridal chamber," a Semitic phrase for the groom's friends and wedding guests. Wedding feasts lasted days, and guests were excused from religious duties such as fasting. In the prophets, God himself is Israel's groom: "your God will rejoice over you" like a bridegroom over his bride (Isaiah 62:5; compare Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus does not explain the image, but by calling himself the groom he places his coming within that hope. John the Baptist uses the same picture in John 3:29, and the church is later called the bride (Revelation 19:7; 21:2).
r: Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20; Jeremiah 2:2; John 3:29; Revelation 19:7; Matthew 9:15; Matthew 25:1–13

a: the groom will be taken away from them
p: The first shadow of the cross in Mark. The verb may echo Isaiah 53:8, where the servant is "taken away."
b: This is the first hint in Mark that Jesus will be removed by force. The Greek aparthē, "taken away," is rare; the same verb in its simple form appears in the Greek of Isaiah 53:8, where the servant's life "is taken away." "On that day" (the older manuscripts; later ones read "in those days," see the variant) may point to the day of his death, and early Christians fasted on Friday in memory of it (Didache 8:1 names Wednesday and Friday). The saying places the controversy stories of 2:1–3:6, which end with a plot to kill Jesus (3:6), under the shadow of the passion.

p: Does the saying set Jesus against Judaism? Many readers now take it as about renewal, not replacement.
b: Unshrunk cloth shrinks and tears an old garment; fermenting wine stretches and bursts old, brittle leather. Christians long read the sayings as a contrast between the "new" gospel and the "old" Judaism, which could not hold it. Many scholars now caution against that reading. In context the sayings answer a question about fasting: Jesus' presence brings a joy that the usual forms cannot contain. Luke even adds that no one who has drunk old wine wants the new, because the old is good (Luke 5:39), which keeps a place for the old. Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine point out that Jesus' "new" teaching is itself drawn from Israel's Scriptures and hopes.

a: As his disciples went making their way
p: The Greek hodon poiein can mean "make a road." Did the disciples clear a path, or just walk along?
b: Mark writes that the disciples "began to make a way, plucking the heads of grain." In classical Greek hodon poiein means to build a road, and a few interpreters picture the disciples clearing a path through the grain for Jesus, like servants preparing a king's way (compare 1:2–3). Most think the phrase here just means "to go along," perhaps influenced by a Latin idiom (iter facere, "to make a journey"). Matthew 12:1 and Luke 6:1 say instead that they ate the grain, and Matthew says they were hungry. Mark mentions no hunger for the disciples, only for David (2:25).

a: Why are they doing something on the Sabbath that is not allowed?
t: What was wrong with picking grain?
p: Picking a neighbor's grain by hand was allowed. Doing it on the Sabbath looked like harvesting, a kind of forbidden work.
b: The Law allowed a hungry passer-by to pick grain with his hand from a neighbor's field, but not to use a sickle (Deuteronomy 23:25). The issue was the day. Work on the Sabbath was forbidden, "Even at plowing time and at harvest you are to stop" (Exodus 34:21), and the Mishnah's list of forbidden labors includes reaping and threshing (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2). Pulling off heads and rubbing them (Luke 6:1) could count as both. Jewish groups disagreed on details: the Damascus Document from Qumran was stricter than the Pharisees. E. P. Sanders thought the dispute, if historical, was minor; others think Mark presents a real clash over who interprets the Sabbath.
r: Deuteronomy 23:25; Exodus 34:21; Exodus 20:8–11; Jeremiah 17:21–22; Matthew 12:2; Luke 6:1–2

p: In 1 Samuel 21 the priest who gave David the bread was Ahimelech. Abiathar was his son. Several explanations are offered.
b: 1 Samuel 21:1–6 names the priest at Nob as Ahimelech; his son Abiathar escaped the massacre that followed (1 Samuel 22:20) and became David's high priest. Explanations of Mark's "Abiathar": (1) a slip, by Mark or by Jesus as Mark reports him, or a memory blending the two names, which also swap in 2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 18:16; (2) epi Abiathar means "in the passage about Abiathar," as epi tou batou in 12:26 means "in the passage about the bush"; (3) "in the days of Abiathar," the better-known high priest of David's reign, who was there at the time. Matthew 12:4 and Luke 6:4 leave the name out, and so do some manuscripts of Mark (see the variant). Scholars across the spectrum discuss this openly.
r: 1 Samuel 21:1–6; 1 Samuel 22:20–23; 2 Samuel 8:17; 1 Chronicles 18:16; 12:26; Matthew 12:3–4; Luke 6:3–4

p: Twelve loaves set out each Sabbath before the LORD in the sanctuary, then eaten by the priests in a holy place.
b: The Law commanded twelve loaves to be set in two rows on a gold table in the sanctuary every Sabbath, "bread of the presence" before the LORD; the old loaves were then eaten by Aaron and his sons in a holy place (Leviticus 24:5–9). When David came hungry to Nob, "The only bread on hand was the Presence Bread" (1 Samuel 21:6), and the priest gave it to him after asking whether his men were ritually clean. Jesus' point is that Scripture itself tells of a case where human need outweighed a sacred rule, and the one who did it was David, the anointed king. The rabbis also discussed this story, and some argued that David's life was at stake (Babylonian Talmud Menachot 95b).

a: The Sabbath came into being for the sake of human beings
t: Made for people: a saying the rabbis shared
p: A rabbinic midrash says almost the same: the Sabbath is given to you, not you to the Sabbath.
b: The verb egeneto, "came into being," recalls creation, when God blessed the seventh day (Genesis 2:2–3). A close parallel stands in the Mekhilta, a rabbinic commentary on Exodus, credited to Rabbi Simeon ben Menasya: on Exodus 31:13–14, he says the Sabbath is handed over to you, and you are not handed over to the Sabbath (compare Babylonian Talmud Yoma 85b). The rabbis used it to justify breaking the Sabbath to save a life. So Jesus' principle was not foreign to Jewish thought. Matthew and Luke leave this verse out, perhaps because it could sound too broad. Codex Bezae and several Old Latin copies also omit it, replacing it with "But I tell you."

a: So the Son of Man is Lord even over the Sabbath
t: Who is Lord of the Sabbath?
p: Jesus as the Son of Man, or human beings in general? The Aramaic idiom allows the second; Mark means the first.
b: If "Son of Man" here meant simply "a human being" (as the Aramaic idiom can), then 2:28 would follow from 2:27: people are masters of the Sabbath, since it was made for them. A few scholars think that was the original sense of the saying. But in Mark "the Son of Man" is always Jesus, and "so" draws a stronger conclusion: the one who has authority on earth to forgive sins (2:10) also has authority over the Sabbath. Daniel Boyarin argues that this is a claim to divine authority, since the Sabbath belongs to God. Christians later moved their main day of worship to Sunday, the day of the resurrection, but Mark itself does not draw that conclusion. See the card.

p: A hand "dried up," probably paralyzed. In 1 Kings 13 a king's withered hand was restored when a prophet prayed.
b: The Greek perfect participle exērammenēn means "dried up," suggesting a hand that had become stiff and useless, perhaps from injury or paralysis. In 1 Kings 13:4–6 King Jeroboam's hand "went stiff and dry" when he stretched it out against a prophet, and was restored when the man of God prayed. Jerome reports that a gospel used by Jewish Christians in his day (now usually called the Gospel of the Nazarenes) made the man a stonemason who asked to be healed so he would not have to beg (Commentary on Matthew 12:13). The man does not ask for anything in Mark; the healing is Jesus' answer to a challenge.

a: Then they could bring a charge against him
p: Jews agreed that saving a life overrides the Sabbath. Whether to heal a chronic, non-dangerous illness was debated.
b: Jewish law agreed that danger to life sets the Sabbath aside: "any doubt about danger to life overrides the Sabbath" (Mishnah Yoma 8:6). A withered hand was not life-threatening; the man could have been healed the next day (compare Luke 13:14). Groups differed on what else was allowed. The Damascus Document from Qumran forbade even lifting an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath (Damascus Document 11:13–14), while Matthew 12:11 assumes most people would rescue a sheep. Note also that Jesus does no work in the story: he speaks, and the man stretches out his hand. The watchers want grounds for a formal charge.

a: To save a life, or to kill?
p: Jesus' question widens the issue: not doing good is a kind of harm. And the questioners will soon plot to kill.
b: Jesus sets the choice as stark as possible. On the Sabbath, the day of rest that celebrated God's creating and freeing (Exodus 20:11; Deuteronomy 5:15), is it right to do good or harm, to save a life or to kill? The word for "life" (psychē) can also mean "soul." Leaving the man as he is would be a kind of harm. The irony is sharp: Jesus seeks to restore a life, while those watching him will leave the synagogue and plot to destroy his (3:6). Their silence answers nothing. Some readers see the question as a challenge to the whole way the Sabbath was being used.

p: Only Mark says Jesus looked at them with anger and grief at their hard hearts. Matthew and Luke leave this out.
b: Mark shows Jesus' feelings more than any other Gospel: anger here (and perhaps at 1:41), sighing (7:34; 8:12), indignation (10:14), love (10:21), deep distress (14:33–34). Matthew 12:13 and Luke 6:10 omit the anger and grief, a standard example in the study of how the later Gospels used Mark. The "hardness" (pōrōsis) of heart recalls Pharaoh and Israel in the wilderness, and Isaiah 6:9–10. Later Mark uses the same word for the disciples' hearts (6:52; 8:17): hardness is not only the opponents' problem.

p: Supporters of Herod Antipas' family. That Pharisees would plot with them shows how threatening Jesus seemed.
b: The Herodians appear only here, in Mark 12:13 and in the parallel Matthew 22:16. They were probably Jews who supported the rule of Herod's family, in Galilee that of Herod Antipas, who had already arrested John (1:14). Pharisees and Herodians made odd partners: the Pharisees had no love for Herod's Roman-backed rule. Mark presents their alliance as a sign of how dangerous Jesus seemed to both religious and political leaders. The five conflict stories of 2:1–3:6 thus end with the first plot to kill him, long before Jerusalem.

p: Crowds come from Jewish lands in every direction, and from Gentile Tyre and Sidon. Only Mark mentions Idumea.
b: The list sketches a map: Galilee in the north, Judea and Jerusalem in the south, Idumea further south still (the old Edom, Herod the Great's homeland, whose people had been forced to adopt Judaism under John Hyrcanus), the land across the Jordan in the east (Perea), and the coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon in the northwest, which were Gentile. Only Samaria and the Decapolis are missing. Mark alone names Idumea. The scene shows Jesus' fame reaching every part of the old land of Israel and beyond, a hint of the Gentile mission (7:24–31).

p: The Greek mastix means a whip. Applied to illness, it suggested suffering sent as a blow.
b: Mastix literally means a whip or lash, and was also used of a scourging. Applied to disease (also 5:29, 34), it suggests an affliction that strikes like a lash, and in the Greek Old Testament it can mean suffering sent by God (Psalm 32:10; Psalm 89:32 in the Greek). Mark does not say these illnesses were punishments; he uses a common word for painful disease. The Plain says "affliction," and the note keeps the picture.

a: You are the Son of God!
p: The unclean spirits name Jesus correctly, but Jesus silences them. No human says it until the centurion at the cross.
b: The spirits' cry matches the voice of God at the baptism (1:11). Mark's readers know it is true; the people in the story do not. Jesus silences the spirits (3:12), and many explanations are given: he refuses testimony from evil; the time for the title is not yet; or, as Mark suggests throughout, the title can be understood rightly only through the cross. The spirits "throw themselves down" before him, the posture of subjects before a king. The first human to call Jesus God's Son is a Gentile soldier watching him die (15:39).

p: Jesus calls the Twelve on a mountain, as God called Moses up Sinai and Israel was formed as twelve tribes.
b: Mark does not name the mountain. In the Bible mountains are places of meeting with God and of founding moments: "The LORD summoned Moses up to the mountaintop" (Exodus 19:20), and Moses later set up twelve pillars for the twelve tribes (Exodus 24:4). Jesus goes up, summons whom he wants, and "makes" twelve. Luke 6:12 adds that he spent the night in prayer before choosing them. Mark's mountain scenes recur: the transfiguration (9:2) and the Mount of Olives (13:3).

a: He formed a group of twelve
p: Twelve men stand for the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus is gathering a renewed Israel.
b: The number is the point. Israel was twelve tribes, though most had been lost since the Assyrian conquest, and many Jews hoped God would gather all twelve again (Ezekiel 37:15–28; Psalms of Solomon 17:26–28). E. P. Sanders called Jesus' choice of twelve a symbolic act announcing the restoration of Israel. The verb "made" (epoiēsen) is unusual for appointing people; the Greek of 1 Samuel 12:6 uses it for the LORD who "made" Moses and Aaron. The purpose comes first: "to be with him." Being with Jesus comes before being sent. Matthew 19:28 has Jesus promise the Twelve that they will judge the twelve tribes.
r: Ezekiel 37:15–28; Psalms of Solomon 17:26–28; 1 Samuel 12:6; Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30; Revelation 21:12–14; 6:7

a: on whom he put the name Peter
p: Petros is Greek for "rock," translating the Aramaic Kepha (Cephas). Mark gives no explanation of the name.
b: Jesus gives Simon a new nickname: Greek Petros, from petra, "rock," translating Aramaic Kepha, which Paul uses in its Greek form "Cephas" (1 Corinthians 15:5; Galatians 2:9). Mark lists him first and calls him Peter from here on, but he never explains the name, and Mark has no saying like Matthew 16:18 ("on this rock I will build my church"). Ancient tradition (Papias) linked Mark's Gospel to Peter's preaching; Mark's portrait of Peter is honest about his failures (8:33; 14:66–72). For the debate over Peter's role in the church, see the card at Matthew 16.

p: Mark translates the Aramaic nickname himself. Its exact Aramaic form is uncertain.
b: Mark keeps a number of Aramaic words and translates them for his Greek readers (5:41; 7:11, 34; 14:36; 15:34). Boanērges is the hardest: Mark says it means "Sons of Thunder," but the Greek letters do not match any known Aramaic exactly. Suggestions include bene regesh, "sons of commotion," and bene regaz, "sons of anger," with "boa-" for bene, "sons of." Why the name was given is not said. Some link it to the brothers' fiery temper (Luke 9:54, where they offer to call down fire on a Samaritan village), others to their bold preaching. Mark's Greek says literally that Jesus put on them "names" (plural), one name shared by the two brothers; English says "the name." It is never used again in the New Testament.

t: Thaddaeus, or Judas son of James?
p: The lists of the Twelve agree on most names but differ here. Luke and Acts name a Judas son of James instead.
b: The four lists of the Twelve (3:16–19; Matthew 10:2–4; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13) agree on eleven names but not the tenth: Mark and Matthew have Thaddaeus, Luke and Acts have "Judas son of James." Many think these were one man known by different names (John 14:22 mentions "Judas, not Iscariot"). Codex Bezae (D) and several Old Latin copies of Mark read "Lebbaeus" instead of Thaddaeus, as some copies of Matthew 10:3 do. The variation shows that the early church remembered the number twelve more firmly than every name.

p: Cananaean comes from Aramaic qan'ana, "zealous." It has nothing to do with Canaan.
b: Kananaios transliterates the Aramaic qan'ana, "zealous, enthusiast." Luke 6:15 and Acts 1:13 translate it as Zēlōtēs, "the Zealot." It may mean that Simon had been zealous for the Law, like Phinehas (Numbers 25:11) or Paul (Galatians 1:14), or that he was linked with the movement of armed resistance to Rome; Richard Horsley and others argue that the party called the Zealots is first clearly attested in the war of AD 66–70, so they prefer the first sense; Martin Hengel argued that the Zealot movement went back to Judas the Galilean in AD 6, which makes the second sense possible. The KJV's "Simon the Canaanite" comes from a later Greek spelling (Kananitēs) and misleads, since he was not from Canaan. See the variant.

p: Perhaps "man of Kerioth," a town in Judah. Other guesses: "assassin," "false one," or "dyer." No one knows.
b: Mark writes Iskariōth, a Semitic form; Matthew and Luke use the Greek Iskariōtēs. The most common explanation is Hebrew ish Qeriyyot, "man of Kerioth," a town in southern Judah (Joshua 15:25), which would make Judas the one Judean among Galileans; John 6:71 calls his father "Simon Iscariot," which fits a place name. Other proposals: from Latin sicarius, "dagger-man," the assassins of the 50s AD; from Aramaic sheqar, "falsehood"; or "dyer." None is certain. Mark marks him from the start as "the one who also handed him over," using the verb of 1:14.

p: Bibles differ on whether "Then he came home" ends verse 19 or begins verse 20. The words are the same.
b: Verse numbers were added in the 1500s and do not always fall in the same place. The KJV and the NRSV print "and they went into a house" or "Then he went home" at the end of 3:19; many modern Bibles and Greek editions begin 3:20 with it. Nothing is missing either way. This site follows the KJV numbering. The Greek may mean "into a house" or "home," and most read it as his base in Capernaum (2:1). Most Greek manuscripts and the Textus Receptus read "they came"; the critical editions read "he came."
orig: Καὶ ἔρχεται εἰς οἶκον (kai erchetai eis oikon)

p: Mark starts the family story (3:20–21), cuts to the scribes (3:22–30), then returns to the family (3:31–35).
b: This is the first of Mark's "sandwiches" (intercalations): he begins one story, inserts another, then finishes the first, so that each explains the other. Others are 5:21–43, 6:7–30, 11:12–25, 14:1–11 and 14:54–72. Here the people close to Jesus think he is "beside himself" (3:21), the scribes say he has an unclean spirit (3:22, 30), and Jesus answers the scribes before his mother and brothers arrive. Placing them together suggests that both groups, kin and religious experts, misjudge him. The outcome is a new family: those sitting around him who do God's will (3:34–35).

t: Who thought he was out of his mind?
p: Literally "those from beside him": usually his family, who arrive in 3:31. Some read it as friends, or as "people" in general.
b: The Greek hoi par' autou means "those from his side," in ordinary Greek a person's family or household. Most commentators connect them with his mother and brothers in 3:31, as Mark's sandwich suggests: they set out to seize him, and arrive outside. Some, including many Catholic interpreters, read it as relatives or friends other than Mary, and take "they were saying" as impersonal ("people were saying"), so that the family came to protect him from gossip. The verse was hard for early copyists too: Codex Bezae and most Old Latin copies change it so that the scribes, not his own people, are the ones who heard and set out (see the variant). The word "seize" (kratēsai) is used later of his arrest (14:1, 44).

a: Scribes had come down from Jerusalem
p: Jerusalem's experts come down to Galilee to judge Jesus' exorcisms. They do not deny them; they explain them.
b: Jerusalem was "up" in Jewish speech, so visitors "came down." These scribes come from the center of religious authority, and in 7:1 another group arrives. They do not deny that Jesus casts out demons; no one in the Gospels does. They give a hostile explanation: he works by the power of the demons' ruler. The same charge of sorcery appears in later sources: the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 43a) says Jesus "practiced sorcery and led Israel astray," and the pagan critic Celsus claimed he learned magic in Egypt (Origen, Against Celsus 1.28). Both are evidence that even opponents remembered Jesus as a worker of wonders.

p: Probably "lord of the dwelling" or "exalted lord," a name for the chief demon. The KJV's "Beelzebub" is the Latin form.
b: The name goes back to Baal-zebul, "Baal the prince" or "lord of the exalted dwelling," a title of the Canaanite god Baal known from Ugaritic texts. Israel mocked the god of Ekron as Baal-zebub, "lord of flies" (2 Kings 1:2), and the Latin Bible and the KJV use that form in the Gospels too. By Jesus' time it was a name for the chief of the demons. If "zebul" means "house," Jesus' reply about a house divided and the strong man's house (3:25, 27) is a play on the name. This site keeps the Greek "Beelzebul."

p: Mark's first use of parabolē: a comparison, image or riddle, like the Hebrew mashal.
b: A parabolē is a comparison: putting one thing beside another. It translates the Hebrew mashal, which covers proverbs, riddles, taunts and stories (Proverbs 1:6; Ezekiel 17:2). Jesus' "parables" here are short images: a divided kingdom, a divided family, a strong man's house. The long story-parables come in chapter 4, where Mark explains why Jesus speaks this way (4:10–12, 33–34). Note that Jesus "summoned" the scribes: he answers them face to face.

p: If Satan were fighting himself, his rule would be over. Jesus agrees that Satan's end has come, but by another way.
b: Jesus' argument works on two levels. On the surface it is a reductio: if Satan is throwing out his own servants, his kingdom is collapsing, so the scribes' charge makes no sense. Below the surface, Jesus agrees that Satan's rule is ending, not because Satan is divided but because someone stronger has come (3:27; 1:7). Jewish hopes of the time expected Satan to be bound or destroyed at the end (Isaiah 24:21–22; Testament of Moses 10:1: "then Satan will be no more"; 1 Enoch 10:4). For Mark that end has begun.

p: Isaiah promised God would take back the captives of the strong. Jesus' exorcisms are that rescue.
b: Isaiah 49:24 asks, "Can loot be snatched from a warrior?" and God answers that even a warrior's captive will be taken back (Isaiah 49:25). Jesus applies the picture: Satan is the strong man, the people he holds are his goods, and Jesus is the stronger one John announced (1:7) who ties him up and takes them back. When did the binding happen? Some point to the testing in the wilderness (1:12–13), others to the whole ministry, others to the cross. The binding of evil powers at the end is pictured in Jewish writings from before Jesus (1 Enoch 10:4) and in Revelation 20:2. See the topic on Satan.

p: Jews said "amen" at the end of a prayer to agree. Jesus puts it first, to stress his own words.
b: "Amen" is a Hebrew word meaning "surely, so be it," said in response to a prayer or a curse (Deuteronomy 27:15–26; Nehemiah 8:6). Jesus uses it in a way no one else is known to have done: at the start of his own sayings, as a solemn guarantee. Mark keeps it thirteen times, first here. The Greek kept the Hebrew word, and so does this site, rather than "truly" or "verily." It signals that Jesus speaks with authority of his own (1:22).

t: The sin that will not be forgiven
p: In Mark the context explains it: calling the Spirit's work in Jesus an unclean spirit. Fear of having committed it is a sign one has not.
b: Jesus has just promised forgiveness of every sin and blasphemy (3:28), and then names one exception: blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Mark alone adds the reason in 3:30: "because their claim was, 'He has an unclean spirit.'" In Mark's context, then, the sin is calling the Spirit's work of freeing people from evil the work of Satan, a deliberate refusal to see God at work. Pastors from Augustine on have taught that it means a hardened refusal of God's mercy to the end, and that anxious fear of having committed it shows the heart is not hardened. For how the churches define it, see the card at Matthew 12 and the topic page.
orig: οὐκ ἔχει ἄφεσιν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα (ouk echei aphesin eis ton aiōna)

a: His mother and his brothers came
p: Mark names them here without detail. Who the brothers were is debated among churches; see 6:3.
b: Mark never mentions Joseph. Jesus' mother is named only at 6:3, where the brothers are James, Joses, Judas and Simon and sisters are also mentioned. Who these brothers and sisters were has divided Christians since the 300s: children of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus (Helvidius; many Protestants today, though Luther, Calvin and Wesley all held that Mary remained a virgin), children of Joseph by an earlier marriage (Epiphanius, the Orthodox church), or cousins (Jerome, followed by much of the Western church). Catholic teaching calls them Jesus' "close relations" (Catechism 500) without binding the faithful to Jerome's view, and some Catholic writers prefer Epiphanius'. Mark's Greek word adelphoi usually means brothers but can cover close relatives. See the cards at Matthew 12 and Mark 6:3 and the topic page.

p: His family stands outside and sends for him; the crowd sits around him inside. Mark's staging makes the point.
b: Mark arranges the scene in space. The family is "outside" (3:31, 32), sending a message in; the crowd is "sitting around him" (3:32, 34). In chapter 4 Mark will use the same language: to those "around him" the secret of the kingdom is given, while "for those outside" everything comes in riddles (4:10–11). Being Jesus' kin by birth does not put anyone inside; sitting with him and doing God's will does. Yet "outside" is not final in Mark: James, one of the brothers, later led the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13; Galatians 1:19), and Mary is with the disciples in Acts 1:14.

a: anyone who does what God wants
p: Jesus redefines family around doing God's will. For readers who had lost their families for the faith, this was a promise.
b: Jesus' answer was shocking in a culture where family loyalty was a first duty (Exodus 20:12). It is not a rejection of family as such: he will defend the duty to parents (7:9–13). It is a new definition of belonging: those who do God's will are his brother, sister and mother. Note "sister": women are full members of this family. For Mark's readers, some of whom had been disowned or betrayed by relatives (13:12), the saying matched Jesus' promise of "houses and brothers and sisters and mothers" in the community (10:29–30). Christian writers from Augustine on have added that Mary did God's will above all, and so is blessed more for that than for giving birth to him.
